newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Key Australian senator faces fresh inquiry.
newsitem.headline: Key Australian senator faces fresh inquiry.

text.p: The Australian senate on Wednesday ordered a powerful committee to probe charges a key senator had misled parliament, but the government delayed the inquiry until a police investigation finished.
Independent senator Mal Colston, under police investigation over allegations of travel allowance fraud, will now face yet another inquiry into his conduct.
He has already been forced to repay almost A$7,000 in allowances after previous senate inquiries found he had misclaimed travel allownces.
Colston, who denies any wrongdoing, blamed that error on sloppy book-keeping by a staffer.

But the Senate on Wednesday voted to refer statements by Colston and the staffer, Christine Smith, over the case to the Senate privileges committee, which has tough powers over the conduct of members.
Smith, after initially supporting Colston's explanation, later recanted.
The government successfully voted down a move by the Labor opposition and the Australian Democrats for the committee inquiry to start immediately.
Government Senate leader Robert Hill said in a statement outside parliament that legal advice warned a simultaneous senate inquiry could prejudice the police investigation.
Colston, under intense political pressure over the fraud allegations, on Tuesday resigned the influential post of senate deputy president, barely heading off a chamber vote to oust him.

Colston defected from Labor last year to sit as an independent and his support has been crucial to controversial government measures, including budget bills, passing the Senate, where the government is in a minority.
But he has now said he will vote against the government, which he accuses of deserting him amid his troubles.
